design_problem.problem_statement: A Locus Robotics LocusOne AMR must navigate a 5,000 m² e-commerce fulfillment warehouse from Receiving Dock A (entry) to Pick Station B7 (120 m path). Constraints: (1) maximum 30 seconds travel time; (2) avoid 12 static shelving units and 8 dynamic obstacles (human pickers moving at 1.5 m/s); (3) arrive at B7 with zero velocity and heading aligned to the station (±5°); (4) payload contains fragile items — no jerky motion (acceleration < 0.5 m/s²). Three engineering layers must be solved: WHERE to go, HOW to move there, HOW to stay on track.
design_problem.real_world_context: Locus Robotics LocusOne is deployed in over 50 warehouses across 6 countries. They report 99.9% task completion rate. The 3-layer navigation architecture (global planning, local planning, tracking control) is the industry standard.

three_layer_architecture.layer_1: LAYER 1 — WHERE TO GO: Global path planning in known static map
three_layer_architecture.layer_2: LAYER 2 — HOW TO MOVE THERE: Trajectory smoothing + local dynamic obstacle avoidance
three_layer_architecture.layer_3: LAYER 3 — HOW TO STAY ON TRACK: Trajectory tracking control

failure_modes.naive_approach: LAYER 1: Plan a path by specifying waypoints in (x, y) coordinates through the warehouse. Just avoid the centers of the shelving units.
critical_questions: The robot is 0.5 m wide. Can it pass through a 0.6 m gap between shelves?
What if the planned path passes 0.05 m from a shelf corner — is the robot safe?
How do you mathematically represent 'the set of all positions the robot cannot be in'?
How does a non-holonomic robot's shape change the set of forbidden configurations?
failure_modes.why_it_fails: Planning in (x, y) space does not account for the robot's physical size or orientation. A path that avoids obstacle centers may still cause the robot body to collide with obstacle edges. The robot's non-holonomic constraint means it cannot pass through certain configurations even if the center point is technically free. Configuration Space (C-Space) is the correct mathematical domain for planning.
failure_modes.failure_consequence: The path planner finds a route that passes 5 cm from a shelf corner. The robot's 50 cm radius body hits the corner, causes the AMR to stop and trigger a safety alarm, blocking the aisle.
failure_modes.scientific_principle: Configuration Space (C-Space): the set of all possible robot configurations q = (x, y, θ) ∈ SE(2). C-Space obstacle (C_obs): the set of all configurations q where the robot body B(q) intersects any obstacle O: C_obs = {q | B(q) ∩ O ≠ ∅}. For a circular robot of radius r, C_obs is the Minkowski sum of each obstacle with a disk of radius r. For non-circular robots, C_obs depends on θ — the obstacle shape in C-Space is orientation-dependent. Free space C_free = C \ C_obs. All planning happens in C_free.

citation.location: Chapter 10: Motion Planning, Section 10.1, Pages 384–398 — C-Space formulation, Minkowski sum, C-obs construction

failure_modes.naive_approach: LAYER 1: In the C-Space grid, find the path using Breadth-First Search — explore every cell equally until reaching the goal.
critical_questions: The warehouse C-Space is 5000 m² at 10 cm resolution = 500,000 cells. BFS explores all cells uniformly — how many cells are explored before finding the goal?
Dijkstra's adds edge weights (distance). A* adds a heuristic. What is the heuristic for a 2D grid?
Why does a good heuristic reduce explored cells from O(N) to O(N^0.5)?
Is the Euclidean distance heuristic admissible? What does admissible mean?
failure_modes.why_it_fails: BFS finds the shortest path only if all edge costs are equal. In a warehouse, paths along diagonals cost more than axis-aligned paths. BFS also explores in all directions equally — it will explore 400,000 cells before finding a goal 120 m away. Dijkstra's handles variable costs but still explores all cells with cost ≤ optimal. A* uses a heuristic to focus search toward the goal, exploring only ~1% of cells.
failure_modes.failure_consequence: BFS path planning takes 45 seconds for a 120 m path in the 500,000 cell grid. The AMR sits idle for 45 seconds waiting for a path — missing the 30-second SLA completely.
failure_modes.resolving_concept_name: Dijkstra's and A* Path Planning Algorithms
failure_modes.scientific_principle: Dijkstra's algorithm: explores cells in order of g(n) = cost from start to n. Explores all cells with g(n) ≤ optimal cost. A* algorithm: explores cells in order of f(n) = g(n) + h(n) where h(n) is a heuristic estimate of remaining cost. If h(n) ≤ actual remaining cost (admissible), A* guarantees optimal solution. Euclidean distance heuristic: h(n) = √((x_goal−x_n)² + (y_goal−y_n)²) is admissible on a grid. A* reduces cell expansions from O(N) to O(N^0.5) in the best case.

citation.location: Chapter 8: Navigation and Path Planning, Section 8.2, Pages 310–335 — Dijkstra's, A*, heuristics, admissibility

failure_modes.naive_approach: LAYER 1 (alternative): The warehouse layout changes when new products arrive. Rebuild the full occupancy grid and re-run A* every time a shelf moves.
critical_questions: If the warehouse layout changes daily, A* must re-plan on a 500,000-cell grid every day. Is there a smarter approach?
What if we don't need the globally optimal path — just a good-enough path through free space?
How can random sampling find feasible paths in high-dimensional C-Spaces where A* would be too slow?
What is the key idea of the Rapidly-exploring Random Tree (RRT) algorithm?
failure_modes.why_it_fails: Grid-based A* assumes a static, known map at fixed resolution. When the map changes (dynamic warehouse), the entire graph must be rebuilt — O(N) computation. For high-dimensional C-Spaces (articulated arms, S-DOF systems), A* is computationally intractable. Sampling-based planners (RRT) explore free space by random sampling, achieving polynomial time complexity in high dimensions.
failure_modes.failure_consequence: Daily warehouse reconfiguration requires 8 minutes of re-planning per robot. A fleet of 50 robots causes 400 minutes of downtime per day — the warehouse operations director halts the AMR deployment.
failure_modes.resolving_concept_name_ar: الشجرة العشوائية سريعة التوسع والتخطيط بالعينات
failure_modes.scientific_principle: RRT algorithm: (1) Initialize tree T with q_start; (2) Sample random q_rand in C_free; (3) Find nearest tree node q_near; (4) Extend toward q_rand by step size δ; (5) If collision-free, add new node; (6) Repeat until q_goal is reached. Probabilistically complete: given enough time, will find a solution if one exists. RRT* adds rewiring for asymptotic optimality. Key advantage: no explicit graph construction — works in C-Spaces of any dimension. Planning time: O(n log n) where n = number of samples.

citation.location: Chapter 10: Motion Planning, Section 10.3, Pages 413–432 — RRT algorithm, RRT* optimality, probabilistic completeness

failure_modes.naive_approach: LAYER 2: Execute the A* path directly as waypoints. The robot drives at full speed from waypoint to waypoint, stopping at each one and then accelerating to the next.
critical_questions: At each waypoint, the robot must stop (v=0) and start again. What is the resulting acceleration profile?
The payload contains fragile glass items. At 1 m/s sudden braking, what force acts on the payload?
Can the resulting jerky path be executed by the robot's control system at all?
What mathematical tool produces smooth position-time curves through a set of waypoints?
failure_modes.why_it_fails: A sequence of discrete waypoints produces a piecewise-linear path with infinite acceleration at waypoints (instantaneous velocity direction changes). This violates the payload constraint (acceleration < 0.5 m/s²), damages fragile items, and exceeds motor torque limits. Trajectory planning smooths the path into a time-parameterized curve with bounded velocity, acceleration, and jerk.
failure_modes.failure_consequence: At the first 90° turn waypoint, the robot's velocity drops from 1 m/s to 0 and reverses to 1 m/s in 0.1 seconds — acceleration of 20 m/s². The glass inventory slides and shatters. Insurance claim is filed.
failure_modes.scientific_principle: Trajectory planning adds a time dimension: q(t) = [x(t), y(t), θ(t)] with constraints v(t) ≤ v_max, a(t) ≤ a_max, j(t) ≤ j_max. Quintic spline: a degree-5 polynomial q(t) = c₀ + c₁t + c₂t² + c₃t³ + c₄t⁴ + c₅t⁵ with 6 coefficients determined by boundary conditions on position, velocity, and acceleration at each waypoint. Quintic splines guarantee C² continuity (continuous position, velocity, and acceleration). Trapezoidal velocity profiles: simpler, linear acceleration ramp — guaranteed bounded acceleration.

citation.location: Chapter 9: Trajectory Generation, Section 9.1–9.3, Pages 340–380 — Spline trajectories, time-optimal planning, smoothness constraints

failure_modes.naive_approach: LAYER 2 (local): Execute the global planned path. Ignore dynamic obstacles — the human pickers should know to get out of the way.
critical_questions: A human picker is walking directly into the robot's path at 1.5 m/s. Detection-to-stop distance at robot speed 1 m/s?
The global path is blocked by a temporary palette. Re-planning the full A* path takes 2 seconds. Is there a faster alternative?
Dynamic Window Approach (DWA): what is the 'dynamic window' and how does it respect the robot's kinematic constraints?
failure_modes.why_it_fails: The global plan assumes a static environment. When a human enters the path, a static global planner has no response — the robot will either stop indefinitely (if safety stop is triggered) or continue on the planned path into the human. A local obstacle avoidance layer operates at high frequency (10–50 Hz) and generates velocity commands that avoid immediate obstacles while remaining consistent with the global goal direction.
failure_modes.failure_consequence: Human picker Mike steps into the robot's path at 5 m distance. Robot at 1 m/s takes 3 seconds to replan. At 1 m/s, the robot travels 3 m toward Mike before a new path is generated — Mike is now 2 m ahead and decelerating, emergency stop triggered, entire aisle blocked for 5 minutes.
failure_modes.resolving_concept_name: Collision Detection and Local Obstacle Avoidance
failure_modes.scientific_principle: Dynamic Window Approach (DWA): (1) Compute achievable velocity window V_a given current v, ω and acceleration limits in time Δt; (2) Sample (v, ω) pairs in V_a; (3) Simulate each pair for horizon T; (4) Score each trajectory: G(v,ω) = α·heading + β·clearance + γ·velocity; (5) Execute highest-scoring (v, ω). Operates at 10–50 Hz, reacts to dynamic obstacles in one control cycle. VFH (Vector Field Histogram) alternative: builds polar obstacle density histogram, selects clearest steering direction.

citation.location: Chapter 6: Navigation, Section 6.2.1, Pages 310–328 — Dynamic Window Approach, Vector Field Histogram

failure_modes.naive_approach: LAYER 3: The robot has a reference trajectory from the planner. Use bang-bang control: when ahead of schedule, stop; when behind schedule, full speed ahead.
critical_questions: Bang-bang control causes the robot to constantly oscillate around the reference trajectory. What is the pattern?
What is the steady-state error of a proportional controller tracking a moving reference?
PID: what does each of the three terms (P, I, D) contribute to the controller's behavior?
How does feedback linearization allow a nonlinear robot model to be controlled with a simple linear controller?
failure_modes.why_it_fails: Bang-bang control produces oscillation around the reference with large position error. A proportional controller applied to a non-holonomic robot's position error directly produces systematic heading error because it ignores the kinematic constraint. PID control adds integral action (eliminating steady-state error) and derivative action (damping oscillation).
failure_modes.failure_consequence: The robot tracks the trajectory with constant 0.3 m oscillation due to proportional-only control. Averaged over 120 m, this adds 40% extra travel distance — the 30-second SLA is violated.
failure_modes.resolving_concept_name_ar: التحكم PID والتخطيط الخطي بالتغذية الراجعة
failure_modes.scientific_principle: PID controller: u(t) = K_p·e(t) + K_i·∫e dt + K_d·ė(t). Tuning: K_p sets response speed; K_i eliminates steady-state error; K_d reduces overshoot. Feedback linearization for non-holonomic robots: define a virtual output y at a point ahead of the robot: ẏ₁ = v·cos(θ); ẏ₂ = v·sin(θ). The input-output map from (v_new, ω_new) to (ÿ₁, ÿ₂) is linear — allowing linear PID to control the nonlinear robot. This is the input-output linearization technique for mobile robots.

citation.location: Chapter 10: Control of Mobile Robots, Section 10.2–10.3, Pages 395–430 — PID control, feedback linearization for non-holonomic systems

failure_modes.naive_approach: LAYER 3: After implementing PID, control the (x, y) position error and heading error independently as three separate PID controllers.
critical_questions: For a curved path, how do you decompose the position error into something a differential drive robot can correct?
The robot is 0.5 m to the left of the path. What steering command minimizes cross-track error?
Pure Pursuit: what is the 'lookahead distance' and what does it trade off?
failure_modes.why_it_fails: Decoupled PID controllers on (x, y, θ) ignore the geometric relationship between lateral error and the steering command needed to correct it. For a differential drive robot following a curved path, the correct command is to steer toward a 'lookahead point' on the reference path. Pure Pursuit geometrically derives this steering command, giving a more natural and robust path tracking behavior.
failure_modes.failure_consequence: Decoupled PID commands full lateral velocity to correct a 0.3 m cross-track error — but a non-holonomic robot cannot move sideways. The robot oscillates left-right while the controller tries to correct the uncorrectable lateral command.
failure_modes.resolving_concept_name: Pure Pursuit and Trajectory Tracking Control
failure_modes.resolving_concept_name_ar: المتابعة النقية والتحكم في تتبع المسار
failure_modes.scientific_principle: Pure Pursuit algorithm: (1) Find lookahead point P_d on reference path at distance L_d ahead; (2) Compute angle α between current heading and direction to P_d; (3) Compute curvature κ = 2sin(α)/L_d; (4) Compute wheel velocity commands from curvature. Trade-off: large L_d → smooth tracking, poor corner performance; small L_d → tight tracking, oscillation risk. Stanley method (used on Stanford's Junior): minimizes cross-track error and heading error simultaneously using a geometrically-derived steering law.

citation.location: Chapter 11: Mobile Robots, Section 11.4, Pages 487–497 — Pure Pursuit, Stanley controller, path tracking

failure_modes.naive_approach: LAYER 3 (advanced): The PID + Pure Pursuit system works well but cannot account for future constraints — it only reacts to current error.
critical_questions: The robot approaches a tight 90° corner. At the last moment, PID applies full braking — the payload jerks. Could we have slowed down 2 seconds earlier?
What if we want to minimize total travel time while guaranteeing the acceleration constraint?
Model Predictive Control: what is the 'prediction horizon' and how does it enable proactive planning?
failure_modes.why_it_fails: Reactive controllers (PID, Pure Pursuit) only observe current error — they have no foresight. They cannot proactively slow down before a constraint (corner, weight limit, human in path) is encountered. MPC optimizes future control inputs over a prediction horizon, finding the input sequence that minimizes a cost function while satisfying all constraints — achieving smooth, constraint-respecting, optimal behavior.
failure_modes.failure_consequence: PID controller reacts to the tight corner at the last moment — full braking at 0.5 m from the corner produces 2 m/s² deceleration, exceeding the 0.5 m/s² payload constraint. Fragile items shift. MPC would have started decelerating 3 seconds earlier.
failure_modes.scientific_principle: MPC at each timestep k: (1) Build prediction model x_{k+j|k} = A·x_{k+j-1|k} + B·u_{k+j-1}; (2) Solve optimization: min_{U} Σ_{j=1}^{N} ||x_{k+j} − x_ref||²_Q + ||u_{k+j}||²_R subject to |u| ≤ u_max, |a| ≤ a_max; (3) Apply only first control input u_k^*; (4) Repeat at k+1 (receding horizon). MPC handles constraints explicitly and optimizes over a horizon N — enabling proactive slowing before corners and smooth constraint satisfaction.
